summary:
Coming from farming families in North Macedonia, we have seen how limited access to useful information can hold back agricultural production, even when modern technology is available. We built CeresGaiaSystems (CGS) to help farmers make more informed decisions about what to grow next.
CGS is an installable web application that combines NASA environmental data with crop characteristics, planting history, and optional soil tests. Farmers select a field, explore up to 15 years of climate evidence, and compare crop suitability and sequences of three future crops. Recommendations explain their reasoning, risks, and missing information; saved records and downloaded reports remain accessible offline.
Built for the Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge, CGS connects changing growing conditions to practical crop-rotation choices. Its goal is to help farmers protect soil health, use water more carefully, and build more resilient livelihoods. We want the benefits of space science to reach the families whose work feeds our communities, starting with our own.
details:
Why we built CGS

Our connection to agriculture is personal. We come from farming families in North Macedonia, where we have experienced how missing or difficult-to-use information can limit agricultural production. Modern technology has created new possibilities, but those possibilities only help when farmers can understand and apply them to their own land.

Choosing a crop means committing time, money, water, and an entire growing season. It also influences the crops that can follow. A useful planning tool needs to connect the weather a field has experienced, the crops already grown there, and the soil conditions that will support the next planting.

We built CeresGaiaSystems to bring those considerations together. Our ambition is to help farming remain a viable, valued livelihood in our country and make the approach useful to farming communities elsewhere. Access to finance, reliable buyers, and supportive institutions also matters. CGS contributes by making environmental evidence easier to use in everyday agricultural decisions.

How CGS addresses the challenge

The Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge calls for decision support that connects NASA Earth observations with local soil information, crop characteristics, and farmers’ circumstances to explore resilient crop rotations.

CGS implements that connection through a field-based workflow. NASA data supplies environmental context; the farmer supplies planting records and optional soil measurements; crop profiles describe growing requirements; and an explainable scoring system compares the available options. Users can choose a target planting month and record whether irrigation is available.

The result is a practical way to explore which crops may fit, how they could follow one another, and what needs checking before planting.

What the application does

1. Builds a record around a field

Farmers select a location on an interactive map, choose a selection radius, and save a named field. Each field has its own planting history, soil tests, and management information. This keeps the evidence and recommendations connected to the land the user is considering.

2. Makes environmental history understandable

CGS requests the preceding 15 complete years of NASA POWER climate data. Where coverage is sufficient, it turns daily records into seasonal patterns and graphs showing temperature, rainfall, hot days, frost, and dry spells.

This helps users examine the conditions behind a crop choice. For example, average rainfall alone can conceal variability between years; CGS also considers rainfall variability and seasonal water needs. Historical trends provide context for adaptation, with their limits clearly stated.

3. Combines environmental evidence with knowledge of the farm

Users can record previous crops and planting dates, identify a currently growing crop, and add laboratory soil results. Soil inputs include pH, salinity, and interpreted nutrient measurements.

These records add information that regional environmental datasets cannot provide. A location’s rainfall history can help screen water suitability, while an actual soil test can reveal a constraint that weather data cannot establish. Users can begin with incomplete records, and the application shows where additional evidence would improve the assessment.

4. Compares crops and plans the next three plantings

The current catalog covers wheat, maize, barley, soybean, sunflower, potato, and tomato. CGS compares their suitability using historical climate, sensitivity to observed trends, soil compatibility, measured nutrients, crop history, seasonal rainfall, and growing-window risks.

Its rotation planner considers the last three recorded past plantings and evaluates ordered sequences of three future crops. It checks crop-family changes, seasonal fit, nutrient-demand patterns, and available soil evidence, with tentative planting windows that do not overlap. Where suitable options exist, it presents a leading sequence and up to two alternatives.

Each step in the leading plan includes reasons, cautions, and evidence coverage. If the available evidence cannot support three crops, the planner reports that limitation. The planning horizon covers three crop cycles; their duration depends on the crops and conditions.

5. Helps users interpret and retain the results

Crop reports show contributing factors, confidence, and information gaps. An optional Gemini assistant answers questions using the selected location, crop history, available NASA observations, and forecasts, and can retrieve additional NASA history when needed.

CGS can also be installed as a web app. After online preparation, users can reopen it, edit saved records, and view previously downloaded data and matching reports offline. Maps, imagery, fresh data, AI chat, and new recommendation calculations require a connection.

How NASA data contributes

NASA data is an input to the planning process and a way to make environmental conditions visible.

NASA POWER supplies the numerical environmental records used in climate analysis and crop screening. CGS uses temperature and rainfall history to assess seasonal fit, water availability from rainfall, and exposure to heat or frost. Other available records provide humidity, wind, solar radiation, and surface soil-wetness context. POWER combines satellite observations and models to provide environmental data for applications including agriculture. NASA POWER

NASA Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS) supplies dated map visualizations, including rainfall, soil moisture, vegetation, land-surface temperature, and wind layers. These help users explore the environmental setting. The imagery is presented separately from the numerical POWER data used in scoring. NASA GIBS documentation

POWER data represents a regional grid, so selecting a field does not turn it into a measurement taken inside that field. CGS combines this regional context with farmer-entered information and labels sources and dates so users can judge what the evidence means. NASA POWER data documentation

Benefits and intended impact

CGS is intended to make informed crop planning more accessible to farmers and agricultural advisers.

·       Stronger planting decisions: Bring climate history, crop requirements, and field records into one place so users can compare options and understand the tradeoffs.

·       Support for soil health: Encourage consideration of crop-family breaks and flag nutrient-demand patterns that deserve attention, particularly when soil tests identify a constraint.

·       More careful water planning: Show when historical growing-season rainfall may fall short of a crop’s reference water needs, helping users investigate water availability before committing to a crop.

·       Greater resilience: Help farmers consider seasonal variability and observed environmental changes when reviewing familiar planting choices.

·       Practical access: Provide a browser-based tool that needs no dedicated farm sensors to get started, with saved records and reports available during interruptions in connectivity.

Our longer-term ambition is to support productive farms, more secure livelihoods, and stronger local food production. These are intended outcomes; improvements in yield, water use, income, or soil condition still need to be measured through field trials.

What makes the approach creative

CGS connects three time horizons in one decision: the region’s climate history, the field’s recent planting history, and its next three crops. This lets users consider how a crop fits both its growing conditions and its place in a sequence.

The project also connects space-based information with knowledge held by farming families. Farmers’ records shape the assessment, while explanations make the result open to discussion with an agricultural adviser.

Uncertainty is part of that explanation. A missing soil test or incomplete history becomes useful guidance about what to investigate next. The core scoring follows explicit, repeatable rules; the optional AI assistant provides another way to explore the available information.

Tools and technologies

·       TypeScript, Next.js, and React: Application interface, server API routes, climate analysis, and planning logic

·       Tailwind CSS and Lucide React: Interface styling and icons

·       MapLibre GL and MapTiler: Interactive mapping, basemaps, satellite imagery, and location search

·       NASA POWER and NASA GIBS: Environmental records and dated map visualizations

·       FAO and agricultural extension references: Crop growing ranges, water needs, salinity references, nutrient-demand profiles, and rotation guidance

·       Meteomatics: Optional short-term weather forecasts

·       Google Gemini: Optional conversational field assistant

·       Service workers, IndexedDB, and localStorage: Installation, offline application access, saved field records, and downloaded reports

 

The project runs on ordinary computers and compatible mobile browsers. It requires no custom hardware.

Design considerations and next steps

We considered accessibility, data quality, limited connectivity, and the consequences of acting on uncertain information. CGS keeps missing values visible, reduces evidence coverage when inputs are incomplete, and excludes stale soil chemistry from scoring. Saved records stay in the user’s browser; cloud backup and account synchronization are not currently included.

The current system is a decision-support prototype. Its crop profiles and scoring rules require local agronomic validation. It does not establish future yields, calculate a measured nutrient balance, or prescribe fertilizer and irrigation quantities. Farmers and local specialists remain essential for evaluating varieties, actual harvest dates, disease risks, equipment, and market conditions.

The next development priorities are trials with farmers and agronomists in North Macedonia, calibration against local crop calendars and soil interpretation, and evaluation of whether the explanations improve planning decisions. Further development could add locally relevant crops, language options, and market or equipment constraints, allowing the tool to reflect more of the circumstances that determine whether a promising rotation is practical.
